title: EU close to deal to link UK carbon market after Brexit split
article:
(Nov 8): The European Union and the UK are in the final stages of a deal to link their emissions markets, a move that would boost liquidity and eventually save companies millions of euros in carbon border taxes.

The agreement, to be announced at a key summit later this month, would enable carbon permits to be traded across the two emissions systems, almost six years after Britain started its own cap-and-trade programme in the wake of Brexit. Negotiators have already ironed out details on emissions caps, supply controls and free permits, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The treatment of financial derivatives is the only outstanding issue.

The EU’s carbon market is the region’s key way to meet its carbon reduction goals. Started in 2005, the market imposes gradually shrinking emissions limits on around 10,000 facilities in sectors from steel and cement to fertilisers, power production and aviation. Once linked, it will allow mutual recognition of permits from both markets for compliance, helpful for companies with operations in both regions.

The linkage deal is set to be one of the main deliverables at the Nov 20 meeting of UK and EU leaders, alongside matching university tuition fees for students travelling between the two. Other areas of agreement include committing to minimizing the effect of their trade measures on vulnerable sectors like steel and electric cars, and deepening cooperation on cyber threats, Bloomberg reported last month.

The European Commission declined to comment on the agreement, in line with its long-standing policy of not commenting on draft documents.

See also: What investors actually pay for

The agreement will not automatically exempt the parties from their respective Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAM), which put emissions costs on certain imported products to shield local producers against competitors from regions with laxer climate rules. Instead, it will pave the way for a waiver once the parties fulfill certain condition embedded in their domestic laws, the people said.

The EU law sets two requirements for such a move: full linkage with its ETS and effective carbon pricing without preferential rebates. Once those are met, the EU will add the UK to a list of countries outside of the CBAM regulation scope via a delegated act.

While the EU carbon border tax became operational this year, with the first compliance deadline set for September, the UK mechanism is to kick off at the start of 2027.

See also: Behind the chair: The art of knowing when not to lead

UK carbon prices have already narrowed their discount to the EU ETS market since the two parties committed last year to establishing a link. The UK carbon contract for December closed at a £64.81 per ton on Friday, while benchmark EU allowances were at €86.55.

The price gap could shrink further over the next two years, as UK allowances move closer to EU permits, Moutaz Altaghlibi, senior energy economist at ABN Amro wrote in a note on Nov 5. That would mean UK firms having to pay more for permits.

“Linking the systems should also improve liquidity, make carbon prices more consistent across Europe, and reduce CBAM-related costs and paperwork for trade between the UK and EU,” he said.

Although the idea of re-linking carbon markets has been discussed for years, Britain’s current Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also working to bring the UK closer to Europe on a broader level.

A key parameter in the agreement will be the cap on emissions in the UK ETS. The EU is set to recognise emissions caps in the British system in the 2028-2030 period, according to people with knowledge of the issue. From 2031, the annual UK issuance will be capped at 7.1% of permits to be issued in the EU ETS.

The UK will also create its own Market Stability Reserve (MSR), a mechanism that the EU has had for more than a decade to automatically control the supply of carbon permits and alleviate a glut of allowances that emerged and weighed on prices. It will start with at least 29.5 million allowances when the deal enters into force.

Before the start of 2030, a decision will be taken on adjustments to ensure that the amount of permits in the UK MSR corresponds to at least 6.7% of allowances in the EU ETS reserve in 2029.

As part of the draft deal, negotiators have also agreed to keep rules aligned over time, with Britain obliged to integrate European rules into its law.

The deal will need to be ratified by both the UK and the EU, in a procedure that involves the European Parliament and member states in the EU Council. It will enter into force a month after the last notification regarding the two other deliverables of the upcoming summit: an SPS agreement on sanitary and phytosanitary standards and a solution on a youth mobility scheme, known as YES.

The parties may also choose to apply the deal on a provisional basis before its entry into force.

title: Stockland scraps Sydney data centre plans after local backlash
article:
(Nov 8): Stockland Corp has abandoned plans for a Sydney data centre following community backlash, in another sign of growing opposition to artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The property developer said the nearly two-square-kilometre logistics project on a former golf course next to Sydney Airport, a joint venture with John Boyd Properties, will “not include a data centre” in its next stage of planning. “We will continue to engage openly with stakeholders as planning for the logistics precinct progresses,” a company spokesperson said.

First announced last year, the development on the banks of the Cooks River has sparked criticism from community groups after data centres were added as a potential alternative use earlier this year. The company had said that the project’s proximity to the airport and nearby Port Botany made it suitable for mixed uses like retail and hospitality.

Community opposition to data centres is growing across Australia on concerns over their heavy power and water use. Last month, data centre company Nextdx Ltd placed development plans on hold after protests delayed power supply to one of its major projects in Melbourne.

Firmus Grid Ltd also faced backlash against its planned data centres. The company was set to debut on Australia’s stock market last month, but shelved plans after failing to win over investors for its US$30 billion valuation.

title: China set to lead world in energy investment in 2026, CCTV says
article:
(Nov 8): China is expected to invest US$940 billion in energy in 2026, the most by any country, according to the Global Energy Transition Report 2026 released by the China Enterprise Reform and Development Society, China Central Television reported Sunday.

China had 2.337 billion kilowatts of installed renewable power capacity at the end of 2025, accounting for 60.1% of its total power capacity and 63.6% of new renewable installations globally, according to CCTV. Renewable generation reached 3.99 trillion kilowatt-hours, or 38.3% of the country’s power output, while additional renewable generation fully covered the increase in electricity consumption.

China’s energy investment focus is increasingly shifting from rapid capacity expansion towards grids and other infrastructure needed to integrate its renewable buildout. The International Energy Agency expects the country’s grid investment to rise to about US$140 billion in 2026.

Coal-fired power’s share of Chinese electricity generation fell to 49.7% in the first half of 2026, dropping below 50% for the first time, the report said. China’s energy-related carbon dioxide emissions declined 0.5% in 2025, while the country supplied 70% of the world’s wind-power equipment and 80% of its photovoltaic equipment, according to CCTV.

title: China raises delegate count to 2,360 for 2027 party congress
article:
(Nov 8): China set a quota of 2,360 delegates for the Communist Party’s 21st national congress in 2027, 60 more than for the previous gathering, Xinhua News Agency reported Sunday, citing the party’s Organization Department.

The delegates will be chosen through 38 electoral units, unchanged from the previous congress. The party said allocations will be based mainly on the number of party organisations and members, while also taking previous congresses’ allocations into account, said Xinhua.

The congress, held every five years, sets China’s broad political direction and selects the party’s Central Committee, making it a key event in determining the country’s top leadership.

The latest rules say the proportion of female delegates from provinces should generally account for no less than their share of local party membership. All 31 provincial-level delegations to the previous congress ultimately exceeded that share, according to an official post-election account.

The rules also call for greater representation of workers in newer forms of employment, such as those working in the digital economy.

Delegates are chosen through 38 electoral units covering regions and parts of the party-state system. Candidates are nominated from grassroots party organisations and vetted through successive levels before party congresses or representative meetings hold the final elections, with contested ballots required to have more than 15% more candidates than seats.

title: Australia home sales rise in fledgling sign of property recovery
article:
(Nov 8): Australian home sales and auction clearance rates climbed, offering hopes of a recovery for a property market that has slumped as interest rates rose this year.

The number of auctions held across the country’s capital cities over the past week increased 1.2% from a week earlier to a total of 1,734, and is set to exceed 2,000 in the next seven days, according to property researcher Cotality.

Sydney accounted for 709 auctions, broadly in line with the prior week, while Melbourne registered a weekly increase of 18.4% to 612 and Adelaide reported 149 — the highest reading since March.

Clearance rates rose 4.3 percentage points to 51.5% after falling to a six-year low last week. The latest reading was helped along by an almost 10 percentage point gain for Melbourne alone, according to Cotality.

The results offer a glimmer of optimism that the country’s property slump, which could be the worst in decades, may be finding a floor as buyers take advantage of lower prices.

Rising interest rates and new tax rules governing property investing unveiled in May have amplified the pullback. Last week, the Reserve Bank of Australia delivered its fifth interest rate increase this year, raising the cash rate 25 basis points to 4.85% — the highest level in 18 years.

See also: Thai spyware alerts prompt opposition leaders to demand probe

title: Meta’s bond sale shows new reality for tech debt
article:
(Nov 8): Selling billions of dollars of corporate bonds on Election Day seemed like a real gamble.

But to Meta Platforms Inc, waiting seemed like an even bigger one.

The Facebook parent aimed to sell US$25 billion of bonds this quarter, and took the unusual step of launching the offering on Tuesday Nov 3, as US voters went to the polls. Breaking with convention may have been the right move, however, as a sweeping victory by Democrats in the midterms now threatens to make financing artificial intelligence investment more difficult and expensive.

The fear is that a Democratic majority in Congress will slow the pace of AI development, cutting into cash flow for companies expecting their data centre projects to generate income. US equities dropped on Thursday, and risk premiums on tech bonds climbed over the week.

Even before Election Day, money managers had become more wary of the amount of bonds that big tech companies known as hyperscalers have sold. As fund managers grow more concerned about the debt, firms looking to borrow have started using the kind of careful timing and communication that is more common in junk debt markets.

See also: SoftBank, ABB said to consider China carve-out to salvage robotics deal

“Investors are demanding a higher premium and much greater clarity on how enormous AI capital expenditure will translate into revenue and free cash flow,” said Jack Daley, a portfolio manager at TwentyFour Asset Management. “Hyperscalers have started to guide the market more on the timings of deals and on when positive free cash flow will return,” added Daley.

Oracle Corp, for example, assured investors on Monday that it was only borrowing US$10 billion, a figure that wouldn’t grow, and that it was selling a similar amount of equity. It had to pay yields a hefty 0.35 percentage point above levels on its existing debt.

Meanwhile, Meta had been looking to borrow in late October or early November to fund its artificial intelligence investments after being largely cut out of the market earlier due to a quiet period before earnings. Later in October, a US$25 billion bond sale from Microsoft Corp complicated its plans by absorbing a large amount of investor capital. On Monday, Alphabet sold €6 billion (US$6.7 billion) of notes, the same day that Oracle borrowed in the US.

See also: US believes woman close to Nvidia CEO a China spy — report

But there was a possible window for a bond sale on Tuesday, Nov 3. Election Day tends to be quiet for markets, as money managers often focus on early election returns and fear taking too much risk shortly before prices might drop.

The tech giant huddled with bankers at Citigroup Inc and Morgan Stanley to debate timing, according to people familiar with the matter. They decided to sell the debt on Tuesday in the US, even if it was unconventional, and then finish the euro deal on Wednesday.

Representatives for Meta, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley declined to comment.

On Monday, Meta began an intensive two-day push where its bankers pitched roughly 500 institutional investors on calls across the US and Europe, the people familiar said, a relatively high number. Meta’s chief financial officer Susan Li personally joined some calls.

The company told investors it didn’t plan to come back to the market for unsecured debt deals until at least the second quarter next year, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private information.

Meta also laid out strategies to diversify the company’s funding base and addressed questions on how AI investments would generate returns, according to the people.

The timing may have worked well, but that’s not to say that Meta borrowed cheaply. The notes due in 2056 — the longest of the five tranches sold — priced at a yield premium of 2.2 percentage points above Treasuries, almost 0.9 percentage point wider than a comparable note sold by Meta in April.

The dollar deal was one leg of a broader fundraising push to help finance its AI ambitions. The firm sold US$25 billion of common stock and raised US$12.5 billion from an offering of preferred shares late last month. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs Group Inc led Meta’s share offerings. The firm also planned to raise as much as US$60 billion through an at-the-market share sale programme, which allows companies to periodically sell shares in the open market.

By Wednesday, Meta had raised another €9 billion in its first euro debt bond sale after drawing a record €53 billion of orders — the most for any corporate deal in Europe.

Questions over AI profitability and the risk of excessive spending have cast a shadow over the technology sector in recent weeks. In late October, S&P Global Ratings revised the outlook on Meta’s AA- credit grade to negative, a first step toward potentially downgrading the company’s debt ratings within the next two years. S&P cited uncertainty around its elevated spending and the impact it will have on leverage.

S&P’s move complicated Meta’s debt sale, delaying a final approval as the company and its bankers waited to assess the impact on Meta’s bond prices, the people said. In the end, the effect was minimal.

The obstacles that companies are increasingly facing with borrowing are a shift from earlier this year. In March, Amazon.com Inc looked to sell between US$25 billion and US$30 billion of bonds in the US as part of a bigger debt offering. It ended up selling US$37 billion of US notes, plus the equivalent of another US$17 billion in euros.

Now, companies are deliberately keeping offerings smaller. Meta’s and Oracle’s latest US dollar sales were below the US$25 billion-plus deals that had become standard.

Democrats notched victories across the country on Tuesday, even in states like Texas that have long been viewed as Republican strongholds. With the House of Representatives and the Senate both turning blue, and governors taking over in states including Ohio, Georgia, Pennsylvania, and Texas, around half of AI data centre additions in the US are vulnerable to stricter local scrutiny and pushback.

It’s unclear how this will ultimately affect hyperscalers. The companies’ bonds broadly rallied on Wednesday as investors prepared for the political pressure on data centres to slow their development of the facilities, and the pace of their corporate spending. That could lead to less borrowing, potentially providing some relief to debt investors.

But on Thursday, tech company bond spreads widened as money managers feared that investments could end up taking longer to pay off in a more difficult regulatory environment. As of Friday’s close, average spreads for tech companies were wider for the week.

The companies’ debt binge remains historic. In the investment-grade market globally, firms and projects have borrowed more than US$415 billion this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

And more deals are in the works: Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Apollo Global Management Inc are in talks with investors to start selling portions of a roughly US$40 billion chip financing deal for SpaceX, which is comprised of a loan and bonds.

title: Binance’s CFO leaves company in wake of US$6 bil crypto heist
article:
(Nov 8): Kaiser Ng, the chief financial officer at Binance Holdings Ltd, the world’s largest crypto exchange, is leaving, the company announced just days after hackers stole more than US$6 billion in cryptocurrency from the platform.

“Kaiser Ng has decided to pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance, with a transition plan implemented over the last six months,” Binance co-chief executive officer Yi He said in a statement. “We wish him the best in his next chapter.” Justin Yek will become the firm’s new CFO, she said.

Hackers stole US$6.3 billion from Binance last week in the biggest heist in cryptocurrency’s history. It came as the industry leapfrogs into the mainstream at a time when the ascent of artificial intelligence presents ever-increasing cybersecurity challenges.

Crypto exchanges Bitget, Bybit and other platforms have also suffered major hacks.

The FBI said on Oct 31 that North Korea was responsible for the Binance attack. The exchange subsequently said it had covered about 90% of the US$6.3 billion, making progress on its pledge to fully reimburse customers.

Ng joined the firm in January 2022, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before Binance, he was at Kraken, another crypto exchange, for about five years. Ng did not immediately respond to a request for comment via Linkedin.

See also: Bitcoin selloff eases as investors explore cautious recovery

Yek was most recently at payments platform Airwallex as vice-president of finance.

“I am thrilled to step into the role of CFO at Binance,” Yek said in the statement. “I look forward to leading our finance organisation as we continue to scale responsibly and deliver on our mission globally.”
